content: Abacavir can cause severe allergic reactions that may result in death. If you develop a rash or at least one symptom from two of the following groups, stop taking abacavir and contact your doctor immediately: fever; extreme tiredness; upset stomach, vomiting, diarrhea, or stomach pain; sore throat, shortness of breath, or cough. Your pharmacist will provide you with a warning card listing these symptoms. Always carry this card with you. If you stop taking abacavir due to an allergic reaction, never take it again. If you stop taking it for any other reason, do not restart it without consulting your doctor. Abacavir may also cause serious liver damage and a condition called lactic acidosis. Inform your doctor if you consume large amounts of alcohol or have a history of liver disease. If you experience unusual bleeding or bruising, loss of appetite, pain in the upper right part of your stomach, yellowing of the skin or eyes, or persistent upset stomach and tiredness, contact your doctor immediately. Keep all appointments with your doctor and laboratory, as your doctor will order tests to monitor your body’s response to abacavir. Abacavir is prescribed in combination with other medications to treat HIV infection in patients with or without AIDS. It belongs to a class of antiviral medications called nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors (NRTIs) and works by slowing the spread of HIV in the body. However, abacavir is not a cure for HIV and may not reduce the number of HIV-related illnesses. It also does not prevent the spread of HIV to others. Abacavir is available as a tablet and a liquid solution to be taken orally, usually twice a day, with or without food. To ensure consistent use, take it at the same time every day. Follow the instructions on your prescription label carefully, and consult your doctor or pharmacist if you have any questions. Take abacavir exactly as directed, without altering the dose or frequency. Continue taking it even if you feel well, and do not stop without consulting your doctor. Before starting abacavir, read the manufacturer’s medication guide thoroughly. Abacavir is sometimes used in combination with other antiviral medications to prevent HIV infection in individuals who have been exposed to the virus. Discuss the potential risks of using this medication for your condition with your doctor. It may also be prescribed for other uses; consult your doctor or pharmacist for more information. Before taking abacavir, inform your doctor and pharmacist if you are allergic to abacavir or any other medications. Provide a list of all prescription and nonprescription medications, vitamins, nutritional supplements, and herbal products you are taking, especially methadone. Your doctor may need to adjust your medication doses or monitor you for side effects. Additionally, inform your doctor if you have or have ever had kidney disease. If you are pregnant, planning to become pregnant, or breastfeeding, inform your doctor. If you become pregnant while taking abacavir, contact your doctor immediately. Do not breastfeed while taking this medication. Discuss the safe use of alcohol with your doctor while on abacavir. If you miss a dose of abacavir, take it as soon as you remember. However, if it is almost time for your next dose, skip the missed dose and continue your regular schedule. Do not take a double dose to make up for a missed one. Abacavir may cause side effects. Inform your doctor if you experience any of the following symptoms and they are severe or persistent: upset stomach, vomiting, diarrhea, loss of appetite, tiredness, or difficulty sleeping. Some side effects can be serious. Contact your doctor immediately if you experience muscle or joint pain, headache, pain or tingling in the hands or feet, swelling of the hands, feet, ankles, or lower legs, pink eye, or mouth bruises. If you experience any unusual problems while taking abacavir, contact your doctor. Serious side effects can be reported to the FDA’s MedWatch Adverse Event Reporting program. Store abacavir in its original container, tightly closed, and out of reach of children. Keep it at room temperature, away from excess heat and moisture (not in the bathroom). Liquid medication can be stored at room temperature or in the refrigerator but should not be frozen. Dispose of outdated or unneeded medication properly by consulting your pharmacist. In case of overdose, contact your local poison control center at 1-800-222-1222. If the person has collapsed or is not breathing, call 911 immediately. Do not share your medication with others. Consult your pharmacist if you have questions about refilling your prescription.
